analytic.title: A Timing Verification Framework for AUTOSAR OS Component Development based on Real-Time Maude

div.p: The AUTOSAR (AUTomotive Open System ARchitecture) is an open standard in automotive industry, aiming at unifying the methodology of the automotive software development. It is drawing increasing attention because of its great concern about the safety of automotive electronics. The safety of automotive electronics greatly depends on the Operating System (OS) components, which fully implement the functionality part of automotive applications. However, taking the complex timing protection mechanism of AUTOSAR OS and random occurrences of interrupt requests (IRs) into consideration, it is hard for the developers to design and configure the OS components correctly or even reconcilably. In this paper, we focus on the timing properties and propose an automatic verification framework, in which developers could analyze the timing behaviors and devise the OS components configuration. Furthermore, three important timing properties are expressed and can be verified in our framework, namely, schedulability, non-fault-propagation, and consistency. As a reduced version of AUTOSAR OS and auxiliary analysis modules have been implemented based on Real-Time Maude, developers could easily employ the tool to experiment with different configurations of OS components.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: With the growing complexity of automotive electronics, it is much more stringent to unify and standardize the methodology of the automotive development. The AUTOSAR Development Partnership is founded aiming at establishing such an industry standard. The AUTOSAR standard is comprised of a set of specifications describing software components and their interfaces. It is drawing increasing attention because of its wide acceptance among the automotive manufacturers and great concern about the safety and quality of products.

The rough outline of the development process in AUTOSAR is described in Fig. 1 [1]. The process is divided into four phases. Firstly, the software components are mapped to certain ECUs (Electronic Control Units) in terms of the resources and timing requirements in the Configure System phase. The information related to a specific ECU is extracted in the Extract ECU-Specific Information phase. In the phase Configure ECU the OS components and other BSW (Basic SoftWare) modules are configured by the OS component designers. All the configuration information is included in a standard XML document ECU Configuration Description. The ECU Configuration Description is the start point of our work from which we obtain the OS component configuration information. Finally, the executable files are generated by the compiler based on the XML document in the last phase. On a specific ECU, the OS components are coordinated by AUTOSAR OS to fulfill the different requirements of applications. Recently more and more approaches to guarantee correctness of AUTOSAR OS using formal methods are proposed. But it is not enough if we only focus on the OS verification. The quality of automotive electronics would still be greatly compromised if we have some insecure components running on the cars, however perfect the automotive OS is. The correctness of OS components should be investigated as well. In fact, a good design of OS components and collaboration among these components is much more reliant on numerous experiments and long experience in this field. It is really unpractical to perform numerous experiments on the final products for reason of time and cost. In addition, the complex context caused by the interrupts makes the manual analysis much more difficult. So we believe it is important to provide the developers rigorous and automatic approaches to verify different properties and help them experiment on different configurations and further improve the design of components.

There should be various ways to verify different aspects of OS component configuration. In this paper, we focus on the timing properties verification. The overall framework can be expressed in Fig. 2. Based on the AUTOSAR OS specification, we model a reduced version of the OS using Real-Time Maude. All the relevant information, e.g. the priority of task, the structure of schedule table, the time frame of interrupt service routine etc., is extracted from the XML document and can be transformed to the initial state of the formal model. As all the XML documents are standardized in AUTOSAR, we can easily parse the documents and automatically transform the configuration information into the input of verification tool. In terms of the AUTOSAR specification, three important timing properties, namely, schedulability, non-fault-propagation, consistency should be guaranteed. These three timing properties can be verified in our framework. We also extend the Real-Time Maude and provide the analysis modules. If there exist some violations, developers can easily track the error traces via the tool and devise the configuration.

The remaining part is organized as follows. In section 2, we give a brief introduction about the rewriting logic and Real-Time Maude. In section 3, we introduce the components of AUTOSAR OS and the scheduling policy of AUTOSAR OS in details. The scope of this paper and a few assumptions are explained as well. Section 4 presents the modeling process on the AUTOSAR timing strategy. The analysis and verification of the timing properties are presented in section 5. A case study follows up to illustrate the whole process and show how our framework is used in the verification respectively. Section 6 outlines related works and section 7 concludes the paper.

div.head: II. REWRITING LOGIC AND REAL-TIME MAUDE
div.p: Rewriting logic [2], [3] provides a flexible and general framework to model and verify concurrent systems. A concurrent system can be specified as a rewrite theory R = (Σ, E, R), where (Σ, E) is an equational theory, and R is a set of (possibly conditional) rewrite rules. An equational theory (Σ, E) defines a set of data types and a set of equational properties. It can be used to model the static part of the system. The rewrite rules R define a set of transition rules of the form t → s and can be used to specify the concurrent transitions of systems. Both t and s can be parametric terms in the equational theory.

In order to specify real-time systems, an embedded Time data type is added to rewriting logic. The global state becomes pairs (t, r), where t is an untimed state and r is a term of type Time. The rewrite rules have two types: (i) instantaneous rewrite rules that do not change the global time and (ii) tick rewrite rules of the form (t, r) → (s, r ).

Maude is a high-level language and high-performance system based on rewriting logic. Real-Time Maude [4] is an extension of Maude with Time implemented in the system. It supports symbolic simulation, unbounded and time-bounded reachability analysis, and linear temporal logic model checking. In Real-Time Maude, time is implemented as discrete one, but it provides sampling strategy to support dense time. The concrete syntax is as follows.

The basic concept in Maude is module. There are two kinds of modules: functional modules and system modules. In functional modules, we can define sorts, operations, variables and equations. These definitions constitute the basic data types in a system. Rewrite rules are defined in system modules, which are used to specify the dynamic part of a system. In Real-Time Maude, all modules are declared as timed modules using the keyword tmod.

Sorts and operations are used to define the static part of a system. Subsort feature defines the hierarchy structure of data types. Op defines the operations on the data type. The syntax of declaring sorts and operations is as follows. op1 is an operation with two arguments. Real-Time Maude also supports timed tick rules. {_} is a built-in construct of sort GlobalSystem with operand t as the state of the system. GlobalSystem is used to assure that the whole system advances time uniformly. n is of sort Time.

OVERVIEW OF AUTOSAR OS This section introduces the basic components of the AU- TOSAR OS and the scheduling policy on these components. The concepts relating to the timing protection mechanism in the AUTOSAR OS are presented as well. In short, the AUTOSAR OS is a statically configured multitasking uniprocessor OS and adopts a priority-based scheduling policy.

div.head: A. Task Management
div.p: The AUTOSAR OS is an extension of the OSEK/VDX OS. The AUTOSAR OS continues to use OSEK/VDX OS task management. Two different types of tasks are provided: (i) basic tasks that have only three states (namely, running, ready, and suspended) and can be multiple activated and (ii) extended tasks that have one more waiting state. The event mechanism provides a way of collaboration. In this paper, we focus on All tasks are created as suspended (except for the autostart tasks). A suspended task can transit from suspended state to ready state by calling the OS service ActivateTask. OS selects one ready task to run according to the scheduling policy. The running task may terminate itself by system service TerminateTask and become suspended or it may be interrupted and become ready.

div.head: B. Interrupt Handling
div.p: Interrupt service routines (ISRs) are invoked on the occurrences of external interrupt requests on the processor. ISRs are subdivided into two categories. ISRs of Category 1 do not use OS services and have no influence on task management. ISRs of this category have the less overhead. ISRs of Category 2 allow all OS services invocation except some services dedicated entirely to tasks (WaitEvent, TerminateTask). Since timing protection mechanism in AUTOSAR only applies to Category 2 ISRs, we do not consider Category 1 ISRs in this paper. But Category 1 ISRs can be modeled by Category 2 ISRs in our model.

Each ISR is assigned a virtual priority which is higher than priorities of tasks. Different from tasks, the activation of an ISR is usually aperiodic. There are also a few differences between tasks and ISRs in the API (Application Programming Interface) invocation. For example, the ISRs cannot call WaitEvent and ClearEvent. As we do not go into the event mechanism at the moment, we can omit the differences. In other words, we can treat ISRs as tasks with higher priorities. According to the underlying processors, one ISR can be preempted by another. The interrupt requests are checked at every clock cycle and only one of them is recognized by ECU each time.

div.head: C. Scheduling Policy and Schedule Logic
div.p: Static priorities are assigned to the tasks in system configuration phase. While several ready tasks may be competing for the processor at the same time, the OS executes the instructions of the task with the highest priority. A task can be declared as being preemptable or non-preemptable. We only consider the full preemptive scheduling policy in this paper when all tasks are preemptable. In normal situation (without interrupt), a non-preemptable task can be executed to the end unless it relinquishes the processor voluntarily.

AUTOSAR OS introduces the component schedule table to deal with the task activation relating to time. Essentially schedule table is an extension of alarm in OSEK/VDX but it provides a more intuitive and convenient way to organize the task activation and event setting in terms of time. The structure of schedule table is shown in Fig. 3. Each schedule table is comprised of a statically defined set of expiry points (EPs). Each expiry point defines one or more actions that must occur after a certain period of time elapses where an action is either the activation of a task or the setting of an event and an offset in ticks from the start of the schedule table. Schedule logic is an abstraction of schedule table as is shown in Fig. 3. Thus we can obtain the schedule logic from the XML document.

div.head: D. Fault Propagation and Timing Protection
div.p: There are many tasks configured on one ECU and scheduled by the OS. One task is easily influenced by the other tasks. For example, too much activation of higher-priority tasks leads to lower-priority tasks missing the deadline. If the higherpriority tasks make a mistake and execute for a little longer than expected, they may still finish before the deadline but the lower-priority tasks may be so postponed that they would miss the deadline. This is called the fault propagation.

The timing protection is a time monitoring mechanism in AUTOSAR to avoid such fault propagation at runtime. A series of parameters about the tasks are statically configured by the developer. When violating the statically configured conditions, a user-defined function will be called to deal with the faulty state. There are three types of timing protection.
• Execution Time Protection. Tasks and ISRs should be finished before a statically configured upper bound which is called the execution budget.

• Inter-arrival Time Protection. There is a statically configured lower bound, called the time frame, on the time of a task permitted to be activated and a Category 2 ISR recognized by the OS. In other words, the task could be activated successfully at most once per time frame and the inter-arrival number of times of Category 2 ISRs should be limited to one per time frame.

div.head: IV. MODELING THE AUTOSAR OS
div.p: In this section, we focus on modeling AUTOSAR OS using Real-Time Maude. Firstly, the way to model the static configuration of tasks and ISRs is given. We can obtain most of the static configuration from the XML document mentioned before. The dynamic part of system state is presented then. These two parts constitute the system context. After that, 8 rewrite rules are introduced to model the transitions of the system context. Additional rules are specified to model the interrupt handling. Note that in our model, we suppose the interrupt being recognized by hardware does not take time.

div.head: A. The Tasks/ISRs
div.p: As we have explained in the previous section, tasks and ISRs can be treated as the same objects in our model. Each task or ISR is defined as a tuple t i = (tid i , p i , e i , d i , b i , tf i ), where p i represents the priority of t i , and e i is the average execution time.d i is the deadline. b i and tf i reflect the budget time and time frame relating to the two types of timing protection mechanism respectively. Except for the average execution time which relies on the experience, all the other parameters can be obtained from the XML document.

We use STATICINFO to record all the information of the tasks and ISRs. STATICINFO is constituted by three elements as described in the following lines of code. The first two elements are the multisets of tasks and ISRs. The third one is a controlling flag indicating the decision whether to receive an ISR at each cycle (1 means the decision has been done). This flag will be rather important when illustrating the interrupt handling, as the interrupt request can only be checked at the beginning of every instruction cycle.

div.head: B. The Context
div.p: The dynamic context of the whole system is expressed in Fig. 4. The element of an active queue is a tuple (tid, prio, remainingT obeExecuted, timeT oDeadline). All tasks that have been successfully activated are recorded in the active queue. It is removed from the queue when remainingT obeExecuted is equal to 0. The tasks in active queue are ordered in terms of priority prio. Only one task is running at each instant of time. The interrupts being handled by OS are recorded in active queue as well.

The schedule logic defines the collaboration of a group of tasks. According to the structure of schedule table, the schedule logic can be specified as a sequence of (timeT oDelay, action). T imeT oDelay represents the time remained to be delayed from the last expiry point. With time passing by, timeT oDelay will decrease and the corresponding action action will take place when timeT oDelay becomes 0.

The monitor is used to model the mechanism of the interarrival time protection. The monitor records all tasks and interrupts that have been activated and the task frames of these components. The elements of the monitor are unordered. Once the tasks or interrupts are successfully activated or recognized, the corresponding time frame information will be added to the monitor. The model of system context in Real-Time Maude is the sort Context. It is comprised by the four parts mentioned above including the static configuration. DEADLINEMISS and contexts with [ and ] are both special states introduced for verification. There is a difference between these two states, which will be explained in section 5.

div.head: C. Modeling the Transitions of System
div.p: The execution of electronics is synchronized by clock signal and the concept of time elapsing is reflected by ticks of system clock. Thus we can confine the time domain to natural numbers. The configuration changes with the time passing by. The changes are modeled in the following ways.

When the task or ISR with the highest priority executes, the remaining execution time remainingT obeExecuted of the corresponding task or ISR is decreased. The timeT oDeadline is decreased with the time advancing. When remainingT obeExecuted is equal to 0, the corresponding element of active queue pops out from the active queue and the component with the highest priority in the remaining active queue begins to execute.

T imeT oDelay is decreasing with the passage of time. when timeT oDelay is 0, the corresponding action should be performed. In our current model, the task should be activated. As stipulated in the OS specification, the inter-arrival number of times of tasks should be limited to once per time frame. If the task to be activated is in the monitor set, the activation will be omitted.

When a task is successfully activated and the time frame is not equal to 0, it will be added to the monitor set. When the time goes by, the time frame should be decreased by the same amount. When the time frame becomes 0, the corresponding component will be removed from the monitor.
In terms of the informal description, these transitions on the system configuration are depicted in the following rewrite rules. s(x) represents the successor of natural number x.

The trace is introduced to analyze the errors which will be explained in the next section. These five rules are all timed rules in Real-Time Maude and will tick the global time by one. With the march of time, remainingT obeExecuted of the task undergoing (i.e. the first one in the queue) and timeT oDelay of the schedule logic will decrease by one as is depicted in the rules. The timeT oDeadline of each component in the active queue will be decreased by one, which is accomplished explicitly by the task undergoing and implicitly by other tasks waiting in the queue via operators deadlineOne and MonitorOne. And the time frame of each component in the monitor will be decreased by the same amount. The third and fourth timed rules are used to remove a task from the active queue as soon as it finishes. When timeT oDelay decreases to zero, expressed as # 0 @ task, the corresponding task will be activated by applying the rule [Activate1] and [Activate2]. Whether the task is in the monitor set or not is indicated by the operator isMonitored. If not, it will be scheduled as usual, otherwise it will transit to a special state bracketed with [ and ]. We use this special state to help check the consistency property introduced in the next section.

div.head: D. Modeling the Interrupt Handling
div.p: ISRs are invoked upon the occurrences of interrupt requests.

The occurrence of the interrupt request is random. The interrupt request is checked at each cycle time by the hardware. Only one is recognized by the hardware and handled each time. The interrupt request is checked when the next cycle begins.

When an interrupt request is recognized by the hardware, OS will check whether the corresponding time frame of ISR is over or not, i.e. whether the corresponding ISR is in the monitor set or not. If the ISR is not in the monitor set, OS will perform the context switch and begin to execute the ISR. Otherwise, the timing protection callback function will be invoked.

The interrupt handling is modeled by conditional rules. when the cycle starts, interrupt request is checked by the hardware. At each cycle, any interrupt request can be received. As we can see from the timed rules, the iFlag is set to 0 when the transition commits, indicating that a new cycle arrives and any interrupt can be received. If an interrupt is received or no interrupt is received at this cycle, the iFlag is set to 1, indicating that the check of interrupts has been performed.

div.head: V. ANALYZING AND VERIFYING THE TIMING PROPERTIES
div.p: In this section, we focus on the analysis and verification of timing properties. As the implementation of Real-Time Maude extends the Full Maude tool, it does not provide a command for exhibiting the sequence of rewrite steps leading to a state found during a search. It also does not support the tracing command such as show path, show search graph and print [5]. The analysis on the results is difficult to perform. To solve this problem, we make use of the framework of rewriting logic itself and implement a more flexible and direct way to trace the execution, as shown in the first subsection. As for the three timing properties of the OS Component configuration (namely, schedulability, non-fault-propagation, consistency), we will explain in the following subsections by firstly giving an informal description of each timing property and each followed by a case study to illustrate the verification process. The analysis on the verification results are presented as well.

div.head: A. The Tracing
div.p: In order to track the error trace and provide the developers with the guideline to modify the configuration, we introduce a new data type Trace to log and record the execution. And thus the analysis based on the verification result can be performed. We will illustrate later how the trace module is used to analyze the results. Idle represents that there is no task in the active queue right now and the system is idle for one cycle. Run(id) represents that the task or ISR whose ID equals id runs for a cycle. ISR(id) means that an interrupt request arrives and has been recognized at the beginning of one cycle, while activate(id) means that task id is successfully activated and added to the active queue. Here, idle and run(id) are events that take one cycle while ISR(id) and activate(id) are both instantaneous and occurs when one cycle starts.

div.head: B. Schedulability Analysis
div.p: Schedulability is one of the basic requirements of a correct configuration. Given a concrete OS component configuration, tasks should be finished before the deadlines. Lots of approaches [6], [7], [8], [9] are proposed to perform the schedulability analysis. However, it is not easy to check this property, especially when taking the interrupt handling into consideration.

With the help of Real-Time Maude, we can exhaust all possible execution paths to find the errors. In the process, some extreme conditions are also included and thus some false positive results may be produced during the process. For example, in our model, an interrupt request may take place at any time and occur all the time. But in real life, some interrupt requests usually do not occur so often. Thus manual analysis on the trace is needed to determine whether the errors indeed exist or not.

In our model, we introduce a special final state DEADLINEMISS to represent the state that the current task misses its deadline. Id records the identifier of the error task. The context will transit to the error state if current task misses the deadline, as is depicted in the following rewrite rule. There are two tasks and one Category 2 ISR involved in the configuration. Task 't1 has a lower priority than 't2. These two tasks collaborates in a way that 't2 is activated two cycles after 't1 is activated, as is defined in the schedule table. div.head: C. Non-fault-propagation Detection
div.p: As tasks may be designed by different vendors, it has to be ensured that the time-critical tasks would not be interfered by other tasks and the composition of different tasks is correct in timing. If execution time of one task is longer than expected (should be shorter than execution budget), other tasks should not be influenced and miss the deadline. div.head: D. Consistency Checking
div.p: From the schedule table designer's point of view, the schedule logic should be reasonable, that is, for all expiry points in the schedule logic the corresponding action should take place when a certain period of time elapses. However, after the composition of all components in one ECU, some action may not happen as the designer expects. For example, the designer of 't1 may give a larger time frame value because 't1 executes too long and the designer does not want it to be activated so frequently. In this example, 't1 may be a task reading data from CAN bus. But 't2 relies on the data updated by 't1. The designer of 't2 designs a schedule table to accomplish the task as shown in initState2. But when the system executes, the designer will find that the 't2 does not always get the right data. The reason is the inconsistent configuration of components. The configuration of 't1 is not consistent with the configuration of the schedule table, which leads to the omission of activation of 't1. Thus sometimes 't1 can not be activated successfully to update the newlyupdated data and 't2 can not get the right data. Although the omission of some activation is not an error sometimes, it may bring some obscure errors to the system. We should provide a way to check this type of inconsistency among parameters after the configuration.

Here we introduce a new special state bracketed with symbol [ and ] to indicate a consistency error. The context bracketed with symbol [ and ] is not a final state. Then it will transit to normal state afterwards. The transitions to the special state and back to the normal are both instantaneous. We take initState2 to illustrate how to check this property.

div.head: VI. RELATED WORKS
div.p: The TIMMO project [10] is a pilot project mainly focusing on the timing properties in AUTOSAR. It is prone to provide a timing methodology applicable at different abstraction levels and throughout the development process. In TIMMO project a Timing Augmented Description Language (TADL) [10], [11] is proposed to specify the timing properties from the requirements to the implementation. In contrary, our approach places emphasis on the verification of OS components and intends to help the developer with the configuration.

Pierre-Emmanuel Hladik et al. propose several formalisms based on the real-time theory and manually analyze the schedulability of components in a reduced version of the AUTOSAR Operating System specification [6]. But in our opinion, the analysis should be performed as automatically as possible and approach should be provided to locate the errors. Libor Waszniowski et al. invest further into the inner structure of OS components in OSEK/VDX and provide a finer-grained analysis on the timing properties [9]. But they do not consider the priority of interrupts and the possibilities that the same interrupt happenes many times. And also the AUTOSAR OS is more complicated than OSEK/VDX OS.

Rewriting logic [12] defines a series of transition rules that can be used to model the transitions of real systems. Real-Time Maude is an effective tool to reason about realtime systems [4], which has been successfully applied to simulating and analyzing scheduling algorithm [13]. Modeling approaches for performing schedulability analysis are proposed in [7], [8], [9]. We prefer rewriting logic for three reasons: (1) rewriting logic exhibits a more flexible and direct way to track the execution and control the tracing; (2) Real-Time Maude provides different reasonable time sampling strategies in the verification process; (3) the scheduling policy in AUTOSAR is formalized as rewrite rules, and rewriting logic is more suitable to perform.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we have modeled the timing-relevant strategies of AUTOSAR OS and demonstrated an approach to analyzing and verifying the timing properties of AUTOSAR OS components based on rewriting logic. Interrupt handling is also considered in the framework. Three important timing properties, namely, schedulability (whether the tasks can be finished before the deadline under a given configuration of OS components), non-fault-propagation (whether the fault of one task will propagate to other correct tasks when different components are composed in one ECU), consistency (whether the configuration itself is self-contradictory) are investigated. As a model of AUTOSAR OS and auxiliary analyzing modules have been implemented via Real-Time Maude, the timing properties can be checked automatically in our framework. Developers can employ the tool to perform the experiments and analysis. The traces can be of great help to track the execution errors due to the erroneous OS component configuration.

In the future work, we are planning firstly to further improve the framework to support the event mechanism. Secondly, in order to make our approach easy to use, we have to develop a tool to extract the configuration parameters from the standard XML document and transform the information to the input of Real-Time Maude.
